topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Comparing density using equal volumes
topics.description: Compare the density of uniform materials by comparing masses of equal volumes, and explain why changing the amount of the same uniform material does not by itself change its density. Distinguish total mass from mass relative to occupied volume; no density formula or particle theory is required.
evidence: Compare equal-volume samples using their masses and justify which material is denser, rather than choosing by colour or total size.
Explain why a larger sample of the same uniform material has more mass but the same density under unchanged conditions.
Reject an unsupported density ranking of unequal-volume samples from total masses alone; request an equal-volume comparison or adequate mass-and-volume information.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain which of two equal-sized solid blocks is denser from a balance comparison, then explain whether cutting one block in half changes the density of its material?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Water displaced by immersed objects
topics.description: Explain that a water-excluding object displaces a volume of water equal to the volume of the part below the water surface, and use this to compare controlled partial and full immersion cases. Distinguish displaced volume from object mass and from water-level height; no density calculation is required.
evidence: Predict equal displacement for fully immersed, water-excluding objects with equal outside volume but different mass.
Explain why lowering more of an object below the surface increases displaced volume until full immersion, after which moving the same rigid object deeper does not add displacement.
Explain why the same displaced volume can cause different level rises in differently shaped containers.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} predict whether two same-sized sealed blocks of different masses displace the same water when fully submerged, and explain what changes when only half of a block is submerged?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Buoyant support and floating
topics.description: Explain floating and initial rising or sinking using upward support from displaced water and downward weight. A freely floating object at rest displaces water with the same weight as the object; a fully immersed object released from rest initially rises or sinks according to the balance. Apply the model to hollow hulls and changed loads without requiring equations or a microscopic pressure derivation.
evidence: Explain that water provides upward support even to an object that sinks; compare this support with weight in a released-from-rest case.
Explain how reshaping the same material into a water-excluding hull can allow enough displacement to support its weight before water enters.
Predict and explain how adding load changes the waterline of a floating hull and why a hull can eventually flood or sink.
Transfer the force/displacement explanation to a fully immersed sealed object at rest without claiming that neutral buoyancy brakes existing motion.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how the same lump of material could sink as a solid lump but float as a watertight bowl, and why adding cargo makes the bowl sit lower?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Pressure in still liquids
topics.description: Explain that pressure in a connected liquid at rest acts on immersed surfaces in all orientations and increases with depth below the free surface. Compare pressures at equal and different depths in the same liquid under the same surface pressure; distinguish local pressure from net buoyant force without calculating hydrostatic equations.
evidence: Predict the same pressure at equal depths in the same connected resting liquid despite differing container widths or wall shapes.
Predict higher pressure at greater depth and identify inward pressure forces normal to surfaces at different orientations.
Explain why a deeper rigid fully submerged object can face greater local pressure without a larger displaced volume or automatically larger buoyant support.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} compare pressure readings beside the top, side and bottom of a submerged box, explain why greater depth matters, and say whether water pushes only downward?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Sensing and acting in physical control systems
topics.description: Explain the causal roles of a sensor or input device, a controller following a rule, and an actuator or output in a supplied physical control system. Trace information separately from the power that enables an action, and distinguish sensing a condition from deciding and acting on it; no circuit-building or program-writing procedure is required.
evidence: Trace a supplied sensor reading through a controller rule to a physical output and predict what changes when the reading or rule changes.
Explain why a sensor alone does not choose or power every action, identifying the controller and powered output in the supplied model.
Distinguish manual input, sensing and actuation in contrasting systems, including a device whose output is visible but whose feedback is absent.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how a distance sensor, controller rule and motor work together to stop a rover, and what would happen if the sensor reading changed but the controller never used it?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Correcting a system using feedback
topics.description: Explain how repeatedly measuring an outcome, comparing it with a target or target band and choosing a corrective action forms a feedback loop. Distinguish outcome feedback from a fixed timed action or an unrelated sensor trigger, and predict how a bounded controller responds to a changed load or disturbance without promising perfect control.
evidence: Identify the measured outcome, target, comparison, action and changed outcome in a supplied closed-loop system.
Predict why a fixed timed action can fail after a changed starting state or load and explain how repeated outcome measurement can support correction.
Distinguish a sensor-triggered action from feedback when the measured variable is not affected by the controlled action.
Explain a supplied overshoot or delayed-response case and why repeated measurement does not guarantee instant, exact or stable control.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why a submarine that checks its depth repeatedly can respond after cargo is added, while a program that runs the motor for a fixed time may miss the target?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Force and travel in simple machines
topics.description: Explain the tradeoff between input force and input travel when a low-loss simple machine performs the same output task slowly. Use supplied motion comparisons to explain why reducing input force requires more input travel, and distinguish this from reducing the energy required. Transfer the relationship across a ramp, a wheel-and-axle lifting device, and supplied wedge or screw models without requiring mechanical-advantage formulae.
evidence: For the same load raised to the same height, compare two low-friction ramps and explain the smaller push and longer travel on the shallower ramp.
Trace input and output travel in a crank-and-drum lift and in a supplied screw or wedge model; explain which motion is traded for a smaller input force.
Reject a claim that a machine gives both less force and less travel for the same output without another energy source; explain why friction can increase the input needed.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why a longer gentle ramp can need a smaller push but a longer journey to lift the same box, and find the corresponding tradeoff in a hand-cranked lift?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Load placement and static tipping
topics.description: Predict whether a rigid supported object begins to tip under gravity using the vertical line through its combined centre of gravity and its base of support. Explain how changing load position, support width or centre height affects the static tipping margin in supplied models. Do not infer dynamic vehicle safety or require numerical moments.
evidence: For supplied centre-of-gravity markers, distinguish cases with the vertical line inside, at the edge of, or outside the support region.
Explain why moving a load outward can cause tipping despite unchanged total mass, and how a counterweight can move the combined centre back over the support.
Compare otherwise identical low and high centres or narrow and wide supports under a slow tilt, stating the no-sliding and rigid-body assumptions.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why moving a load farther out on a stationary model crane can tip it even when the load weighs the same, and use a supplied combined balance-point marker to show how to prevent that?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Contact force spread over an area
topics.description: Explain average contact pressure qualitatively by comparing normal force and the area over which it is spread. Predict the direction of change when one factor is held fixed, and recognise when changing both factors requires more information. Apply controlled comparisons to indentation in the same yielding surface without treating pressure as identical to total force.
evidence: Predict lower average pressure when the same normal force is spread over a larger contact area.
Predict higher average pressure when force increases over the same contact area.
Reject a ranking based on footprint alone when loads also differ, and distinguish contact area from the visible outline of an object.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why the same model load presses less strongly per patch when it rests on broad pads than narrow pads, and why two different loads cannot be compared from pad width alone?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Solar-panel orientation and light capture
topics.description: Explain why the orientation of a fixed-area photovoltaic panel relative to direct incoming light can change the light it intercepts and its electrical output. Compare controlled orientations and distinguish facing the current light direction from a fixed tilt chosen for energy over a day or year; no semiconductor theory, trigonometry or installation design is required.
evidence: With direct-light direction, intensity, panel and electrical load fixed, predict greater intercepted light when the panel face is more square-on to the rays than when it is nearly edge-on.
Use controlled power readings to explain the orientation comparison without attributing it to a change in battery capacity or panel area.
Explain why a single angle cannot maximise instantaneous direct-light capture for every changing light direction, and why clouds or shading complicate the simple comparison.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} compare a small panel facing a fixed lamp with the same panel turned nearly edge-on, explain the difference in captured light, and say why the best direction may change as the light source moves?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Shape and floating
topics.description: Use controlled observations to explain that reshaping the same amount of a waterproof material can change whether the whole object floats or sinks. Distinguish a change in shape from a change in material or amount, and reject material-name-only or heavier-means-sinks rules using the supplied comparisons. No density, displacement or force explanation is required.
evidence: Identify a floating object as supported at the water surface after release, rather than held by a hand or resting on the bottom.

In a repeated lump–watertight-hull–lump comparison with the same material and amount, identify shape as the changed feature and use the outcomes to show that the material name alone does not settle flotation.
Transfer the same-material reasoning to another supplied controlled comparison, while saying that an untested hull is not guaranteed to float.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain what changed when the same piece of waterproof modelling material sank as a lump but floated as a watertight bowl, then explain why that does not mean every bowl will float?

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Using a compass to find directions
topics.description: Use a supplied magnetic compass to establish a local magnetic-north reference and identify north, east, south and west in a bounded familiar space. Re-establish the reference after turning the body, and point toward a requested direction without confusing the needle with the fixed case markings. No map reading, numerical bearing or magnetic-field explanation is required.
evidence: Hold the supplied compass level, allow the needle to settle and identify its north-seeking end using the instrument key.
Align the marked cardinal reference with that end and point to each of the four directions relative to the same observation point.
After changing facing direction, re-establish the reference and retain the same environmental directions instead of calling forward north.
topics.assessmentPrompt: With a suitable compass in a familiar supervised space, can {{name}} find north and point east, then turn around and find the same directions again without treating the way they face as north?

topics.subject: Performing Arts
topics.name: Sound and silence durations against a pulse
topics.description: Perform and compare short sequences of sustained sound and silence lasting one or two intervals of a supplied steady pulse. Preserve the relative durations and the entry after a rest when the pulse changes speed. No pitch matching, conventional note symbols or staff reading is required.
evidence: Sustain one continuous sound for one or two pulse intervals, distinguishing a two-interval sound from two separate attacks.
Keep a one- or two-interval silence within a supplied sequence and resume at its specified boundary rather than omit the rest.
Perform a fresh sequence at a second comfortable pulse speed, retaining the relative lengths while actual elapsed seconds change.
topics.assessmentPrompt: With you keeping a steady pulse, can {{name}} make one sound last two pulses, stay silent for one, and start the next sound at the right time, then keep those lengths when you change the speed?

topics.subject: Français
topics.name: Comprendre les relations dans une phrase orale
topics.description: Interpret who does what to whom in a short newly combined spoken French sentence built from a declared taught vocabulary and present-tense subject–verb–object pattern. Demonstrate the relationship by arranging or selecting a scene without needing to read, translate into French or repeat the sentence. Word recognition alone is insufficient.
evidence: Identify agent, action and recipient in a new spoken sentence made from known words.
Distinguish sentences using the same words with agent and recipient exchanged, and change the represented scene accordingly.
Transfer to a different combination and speaker, with the vocabulary, structure and permitted repetition kept explicit.
topics.assessmentPrompt: After the words and sentence pattern are familiar, can {{name}} show who is helping whom when they hear “Mila aide Sami”, then change the scene for “Sami aide Mila”, without seeing the sentence written down?

topics.subject: Français
topics.name: Lire des correspondances graphème–phonème françaises
topics.description: Use a declared taught set of French spelling-to-sound correspondences to decode fresh regular syllables or short decodable strings, rather than retrieve a memorised whole-word pronunciation. Preserve the taught u/ou contrast while combining it with known consonants. The claim is decoding, not guessing a unique spelling from a sound or understanding a message.
evidence: Identify the taught spelling units in a printed item, treating ou as one unit rather than two independent letter sounds.
Blend a new combination of the taught units while preserving the u/ou sound distinction of the target French model.
Apply the same correspondences to unfamiliar explicitly labelled practice strings and explain which changed printed unit changed the pronunciation.
topics.assessmentPrompt: After learning French m, p, a, i, u and ou, can {{name}} read fresh practice syllables such as mou and mu, then combine the same units in a new practice string without hearing it first?

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two equal-volume blocks A and B have masses 20 g and 40 g. A larger block C made from the same uniform material as A has twice its volume and mass. Rank the material densities and explain whether cutting B into two equal pieces changes its material density.
assess.correctAnswer: B is denser than A; C has the same material density as A. Cutting B changes the mass and volume of each piece together, not its material density. Comparisons assume unchanged material and conditions.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Matched-volume and changed-amount cases distinguish relational reasoning from heavier-means-denser or smaller-means-lighter-density rules.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two sealed rigid blocks have the same outside volume but different masses. Both are held fully underwater in turn. Compare the displaced volumes. Then lower one block deeper without changing its shape. Does displacement increase? Explain, and contrast with lowering a half-immersed block to full immersion.
assess.correctAnswer: Equal fully immersed outside volumes displace equal water. Moving the unchanged fully submerged block deeper does not increase displaced volume; immersing more of a partly submerged block does. Water-level rises also depend on container shape.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Mass and depth vary independently of immersed volume, exposing reliance on weight or depth instead of the stated geometric relation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A watertight bowl floats at rest. The same material and mass pressed into a compact lump sinks. Explain both using weight and displaced water. Predict what happens to the bowl waterline when cargo is added, and explain whether the sinking lump still receives upward support.
assess.correctAnswer: The bowl excludes enough water to balance its weight before flooding; the compact lump cannot displace enough water for that balance when fully immersed. The sinking lump still receives support. Added cargo makes the floating bowl settle deeper until support matches total weight, if sufficient unflooded hull remains.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Same-material and changed-load comparisons rule out simple light-floats and shape-magic accounts, while the sinking case tests whether buoyancy is understood as support rather than an outcome label.
